items.title: 6 killed in N. India road mishap
text: NEW DELHI, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- Six people were killed and two others injured when their car collided head on with a heavy vehicle coming from the opposite direction in India's northern state of Uttar Pradesh in the early hours of Monday, local police confirmed.
The road mishap was reported from the state's Kushinagar district. The victims were returning after attending a pre-wedding function at one of their relatives' houses.
The two injured boys, aged 12 and 17, were admitted to a local hospital.  ■

items.title: Highway collision kills 2, injures 3 in Afghanistan's Laghman province
text: KABUL, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- At least two people were killed and three others injured in a highway collision in eastern Afghanistan's Laghman province on Sunday evening, the provincial police office reported.

The accident took place when a Hino truck collided with a rickshaw coming from the opposite direction in the Azizkhan Kas region, along the highway linking the capital Kabul to the eastern provinces, according to the police statement.
Reckless driving was cited as the primary cause of the incident, said the office, adding that the injured were taken to the Laghman provincial hospital for treatment.

Deadly road accidents remain a persistent issue in war-torn Afghanistan, often attributed to deteriorating road conditions, reckless driving, and inadequate safety measures amid challenging terrain and limited infrastructure.  ■

items.title: Philippine police arrest senior figure of Japanese telecom fraud syndicate
text: MANILA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Philippine authorities have arrested a suspected senior figure of a Japanese telecom fraud and theft syndicate that has targeted elderly people in recent years, local media reported on Saturday.

According to local media Inquirer.net, the 57-year-old Japanese suspect, believed to be the syndicate's second-in-command, was arrested by police and immigration personnel in Nueva Ecija province, north of Manila.

Philippine police said the suspect has been regarded as the top leader of the group, known as JP Dragon, since its former head was arrested in the Philippines in June last year. The group has been linked to theft and telecom fraud activities across Asia.

In recent years, Philippine police have stepped up their crackdown on telecom fraud. JP Dragon is also linked to the "Luffy" crime group, which carried out fraud and robberies across Japan between 2021 and 2023 and whose key members were also arrested in the Philippines.  ■

text: TEHRAN -- Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has ordered that any level and kind of threat from the "enemies" must be met with an "immediate and effective" response without geographical limitations, according to a statement published on the leader's website on Saturday.

He made the remarks at a meeting with the Iranian armed forces' senior commanders, including Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces Ali Abdollahi, Army's Chief Commander Amir Hatami, Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Ahmad Vahidi, the statement said. (Iran-Supreme Leader-Order)

items.title: China unveils detailed plan for manned moon landing
text: BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China will adopt a "two launches, lunar orbit rendezvous" architecture for its manned lunar exploration program, a senior engineer said on Saturday, as development work for lunar landing advances steadily.
Wang Xiang, deputy chief designer of China's manned space program and chief designer of the lunar exploration program, outlined the plan at the 7th Manned Space Symposium in Beijing.

Under the scheme, two rockets would separately send the Lanyue lunar lander and Mengzhou crewed spaceship into the Earth-moon transfer orbit, and the two spacecraft would perform a rendezvous and docking in the lunar orbit. Astronauts would then transfer from the Mengzhou spaceship into the Lanyue lander for the descent to the lunar surface and subsequent scientific work.

Wang said the approach matches China's existing technical capabilities and infrastructure, and the separate development of the spaceship and lunar lander can help standardize production and support the formation of a long-term family of vehicles.
While the plan also presents considerable challenges, Wang said the new system for mobilizing resources nationwide is the fundamental advantage for addressing them.

He said the program has established system plans, technical standards and quality requirements under a single development framework, and has adopted an integrated design approach with emphasis on interface verification between subsystems.
So far, the development of the Long March-10 carrier rocket, the Mengzhou crewed spaceship and the Lanyue lunar lander has been progressing smoothly.

Major tests already completed include the Mengzhou spaceship's zero-height abort and maximum dynamic pressure escape tests, the Lanyue lander's landing and takeoff test, plus the low-altitude demonstration and validation test for the Long March-10 rocket.

Wang said future lunar exploration should follow the principle of building knowledge and capability before moving into resource utilization, with a prolonged survey phase needed to understand the moon in a steady, step-by-step manner.

He added that manned lunar landing and unmanned lunar exploration share many common elements in key technologies, infrastructure and personnel, and that achievements from the Chang'e lunar exploration program will also support the manned landing effort.  ■

items.title: 人民网蒙文版
Joint Mideast peace efforts urged
text: The Middle East and the Gulf region should not become a wrestling arena for major-country rivalry or geopolitical conflicts, President Xi Jinping said on Monday, reiterating China's commitment to working with Arab states and countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council to strive for lasting peace in the region.

Xi made the remarks during talks with Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman, who was on a state visit to China from Sunday to Monday. This was the first visit to China by an Omani head of state since diplomatic ties were established 48 years ago.
Xi said that concerted efforts are needed by all parties to foster and safeguard peace and stability in the Middle East and the Gulf region.
China has consistently been committed to ending hostility and promoting peace in the Middle East, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the region's security dilemmas, he said.

The nation will continue to advocate resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means and will support countries in the region in building a common homeland of good neighborliness, development, security and cooperation, Xi added.

He expressed China's willingness to strengthen communication and coordination with Oman and other Arab countries to work together toward restoring peace and tranquility in the region and achieving lasting security and stability.
The Omani sultan said China plays an indispensable leading role in maintaining world peace and stability.

Oman highly appreciates China's just stance on the Middle East issue and is willing to closely coordinate with China to uphold international law, advocate for the peaceful resolution of disputes, and jointly promote regional and global security and stability, he said.

In a joint statement released on Monday on deepening the China-Oman strategic partnership, both countries expressed their encouragement for the United States and Iran to adhere to peaceful options, achieve a comprehensive ceasefire and cessation of hostilities early, and resume dialogue and negotiations to reach a comprehensive agreement.

Both countries also maintain that the situation in the Strait of Hormuz should return to normal and safe navigation be restored, the statement said, and they agree to maintain communication related to the strait.

China has played a positive role on the Middle East issue. While meeting with Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in Beijing in April, Xi put forward a four-point proposal on promoting peace and stability in the Middle East.

He called for adhering to the principle of peaceful coexistence, the principle of national sovereignty, the principle of international rule of law, and a coordinated approach to development and security.

On Monday, Foreign Minister Wang Yi met in Beijing with Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, emphasizing that dialogue and negotiation are the only viable solutions to the ongoing Middle East conflict.

items.title: Draft amendment seeks to strengthen protection of rights in criminal proceedings
text:
By Cao Yin | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-02 16:48

The rights of participants in judicial procedures in China — including victims, suspects, defendants, and lawyers — are set to receive enhanced protection under a draft revision currently being reviewed by Chinese lawmakers.

This draft amendment to the Criminal Procedure Law was submitted on Monday to the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, China's top legislative body, for review.

The draft amendment allows victims or their close relatives to apply for legal aid if they have not hired a lawyer for specific reasons. It also clarifies that if a suspect or defendant hires their own lawyer after a legal aid agency has already assigned one, the services of the assigned lawyer should conclude.

The draft amendment aims to strengthen the rights of lawyers to meet with their clients, mandating that detention centers facilitate meetings between lawyers and detainees within 48 hours of a request. Additionally, it requires relevant authorities to keep lawyers informed at each stage and key points of case proceedings.

Furthermore, the draft revision includes provisions to ensure fair treatment for foreign suspects and defendants and seeks to improve the handling of cases involving children. For example, when interviewing juvenile victims and witnesses, it emphasizes protecting their privacy and reputation and aims to complete the questioning in a single session to prevent the stress of repeated questioning.

items.title: Shanxi art teacher creates Great Wall image with red sorghum
text:
By Zhu Xingxin in Taiyuan and Duan Jinxian | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-02 09:57
An art teacher from Jiexiu, Shanxi province, has recently gone viral for creating an image of the Great Wall by arranging red sorghum grains on the ground.
The creator, surnamed Liang, said it took him five to six hours to finish the piece.
His grandma, now 80, has never been to the Great Wall. Liang hoped to fulfill her wish by bringing the iconic structure to her doorstep.

items.title: Self-governance of Party seen as strategic task
text: Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, has emphasized the need to persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance to maintain the Party's advanced nature and integrity, consolidate its long-term governing position and provide strong guarantees for building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through Chinese modernization.

The remarks were made in Xi's explanation of a draft resolution on certain major issues concerning persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, and were delivered at the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, which concluded last week in Beijing.
Both the explanation and the resolution, adopted at the plenum, were made public on Sunday.

Explaining the choice of the plenum's agenda, Xi said that the CPC Central Committee made this major decision based on its assessment and thorough consideration of the situation and in light of the historical stage that the cause of the Party and the country has entered and the advancement of Chinese modernization as a whole.

Xi said full and rigorous Party self-governance is a long-term strategic task, noting that problems and hidden dangers threaten to undermine the Party's advanced nature, weaken its integrity and jeopardize its long-term governance.

He also stressed the need to consolidate and develop the sound political situation in which great solidarity and unity are maintained across the whole Party, and great cohesion is secured within the Party and the military and among the people.

In the face of complicated international and domestic landscapes, Xi said that persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance is essential for fulfilling the Party's historic mission and ensuring steady and sustained progress in the cause of the Party and the country.
A document drafting group headed by Xi was established by the CPC Central Committee in January this year and held its first general meeting on Feb 6, officially starting the drafting work.
Xi said the CPC Central Committee promoted full democratic engagement, conducted thorough surveys and studies, and sought extensive input during drafting.
On Jan 31, the CPC Central Committee issued a notice soliciting opinions from localities and departments on the plenum's topic and entrusted 16 organizations to research 23 major issues.
Xi presided over a symposium in Shanghai on May 6 to hear opinions from principal leaders of some provinces, autonomous regions and municipalities directly under the central government.

On Aug 3, a draft resolution was issued to certain Party members for feedback, including retired senior Party officials. Dedicated meetings were also held to solicit views from the central committees of other political parties in China, leaders of the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce, and prominent figures without party affiliation.
The Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee met three times and the Political Bureau met twice to review and revise the draft before its submission to the plenum.

items.title: Phantom Blade Zero debuts strongly
text: China's second homegrown AAA blockbuster, Phantom Blade Zero, made a strong debut on Oct 29, reinforcing expectations that domestically developed premium games could become a sustainable growth engine for the country's gaming industry following the success of Black Myth: Wukong.
Developed and published by Beijing-based S-GAME, the third-person action role-playing game topped Steam's global bestseller chart on launch day.
According to SteamDB, peak concurrent players on the platform surpassed 730,000 on release day.

The game is priced at 268 yuan ($40.2) for the standard edition and 328 yuan for the deluxe edition, matching the pricing strategy adopted by Black Myth: Wukong. The project reportedly cost between 300 million yuan and 400 million yuan to develop.

The strong launch has raised hopes that China can build on the momentum created by Black Myth: Wukong, which became a global hit in 2024 and demonstrated that Chinese developers could compete in the premium single-player gaming market.

Ahead of the launch, the title received an average score of 88 on review aggregator Metacritic across dozens of media outlets. By comparison, Black Myth: Wukong carried a pre-launch Metacritic score of 81.

Set in a world that combines traditional Chinese wuxia with futuristic "kung-fu punk" aesthetics, the game mixes martial arts, qi-powered devices and industrial landscapes to appeal to both domestic and overseas audiences.
Despite the strong debut, analysts cautioned that Phantom Blade Zero still faces a challenging path in matching the commercial success of its predecessor.

Veteran internet analyst Ding Daoshi told The Time Weekly that the gap in market scale remains significant. Black Myth: Wukong recorded a peak of more than 2.41 million concurrent Steam players on launch day, roughly 3.3 times the peak achieved by Phantom Blade Zero.

items.title: China’s Manufacturing Activity Returns to Contraction
text: China’s manufacturing activity returned to contraction in October as domestic and overseas demand weakened.

The official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) fell to 49.3, while the nonmanufacturing PMI, covering services and construction, dropped to 49.7, the National Bureau of Statistics said Saturday.
Both fell below the 50 threshold separating expansion from contraction, dragging the composite PMI to 49.7.

Manufacturing weakness reflected a pullback in overseas Christmas-related orders after September, as well as softer domestic consumption following the National Day holiday, the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing said. New export orders and new orders for consumer goods both contracted.

items.title: China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
text: China’s latest viral reality show is about broken friendships — rather than failing romance — between celebrities.

“I Miss You” surpassed 100 million views within two days of its Oct. 22 debut, and topped the real-time TV popularity chart on Chinese review platform Douban since last Thursday. Topics related to the show have repeatedly trended on the microblogging platform Weibo since airing.
Produced by streaming platform Mango TV, the show brings together four pairs of celebrities who have reportedly fallen out for an 18-day trip through the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region.

The show is widely seen as a riff on China’s popular relationship reality shows and follows a similar format to “See You Again,” whose fifth season aired in late 2025, which takes celebrity couples in troubled marriages on an 18-day trip before they decide whether to divorce.

In “I Miss You,” guests discuss their former friendships as a group and one-on-one with their ex-friends, play games, and share their feelings with the production team. A panel of celebrities, a psychologist, and a journalist comment on their interactions.

The most discussed pair on “I Miss You” so far has been Xu Fei and Li Na, two contestants from the 2006 season of “Super Girl,” a popular televised singing competition regarded as a cornerstone of China’s fan culture.

The two were close friends during the competition 20 years ago, but their friendship later collapsed after Li came to believe that Xu had reported her to their management company for taking outside jobs in violation of her contract. Li said the company subsequently stopped arranging work for her, which she sees as having dealt a major blow to her career. Xu denied the accusation, instead blaming a third person.
As the two revisited their past on the show, their memories of their friendship moved many viewers, with one highly upvoted comment describing their relationship as “an epic saga of love and hate.”

Xu said in tears that she had loved “wasting time together,” and noted that her current preferred snacks are the “ones Li loved back then.” Li also recalled how, even when the two appeared to be bitter enemies, they would sometimes end up crying in each other’s arms after getting drunk at gatherings.
Yet the two remained at odds over the past accusation. During an interview with the production team, Li said she had hated Xu “for a long time,” at one point shouting, “What about the money I lost?”

The other three pairs of celebrities include an actor who cut ties with a longtime producer friend after feeling pressured to accept a role, an actress and a writer who fell out when the latter grew closer to a third person, and former professional esports teammates who fought over training strategies, eventually leading one to leave the team.

“‘I Miss You’ feels so much more pure than ‘See You Again,’” read a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that received almost 3,700 likes. “In a marriage, you have to argue about more than feelings. There’s property, children, parents, and so much else. With friendship, we can sit down and focus on just one thing: how we feel about each other.”

items.title: Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019200/Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
text: Many assume the writing is on the wall for human typographers. For decades, the industry has been slowly decimated by the advance of digital publishing software. Now, artificial intelligence is here to finish off the job.

That view has only strengthened since the launch of OpenAI’s Image 2.0 earlier this year. Until then, type designers and typographers had clung to the hope that AI would never be able to replace them: AI-generated fonts and layouts had always looked clunky, inconsistent, error-ridden, or somehow just a bit off.

But Image 2.0’s capabilities took many by surprise: it was able to produce beautifully designed documents featuring long passages of text in multiple languages, while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. The work was not as good as that produced by professional type designers, but for a layperson looking to make a poster or a brochure, it was just fine.

Suddenly, typography — perhaps the last stronghold of graphic design still firmly controlled by professional designers — looked at risk of falling as well. If everyone can generate typefaces and layouts with a simple prompt, or even ask a frontier AI model to operate design software on its own — just as non-programmers can now “write code” through vibe coding — how many designers will lose their jobs?

In the English-speaking world, the AI revolution may indeed prove to be a hammer blow for the typography community. But things are likely to play out a little differently in China: the relationship between text and technology has always been more complex due to the nature of its writing system.

Most contemporary typographic practice derives from movable-type printing technology. Developed in medieval Germany, typography is closely tied to the inherent characteristics of the Latin alphabet: there are only a few dozen letters, and the same letters recur constantly throughout a printed text.

With these characteristics in mind, Johannes Gutenberg developed an entire technological process of carving, reproducing, retrieving, and repeatedly reusing individual letter forms. Once a complete set of letters had been produced, it could be used to print texts containing vast numbers of repetitions of exactly the same glyphs.

Gutenberg would later be credited as a pioneer of movable type printing, a technology whose logic has been carried intact from books to the screen you are now looking at. But applying this technique to Chinese characters is a huge challenge, as there is such a vast number of them. While function words such as de may appear repeatedly on a single page, most characters may occur only once or twice in a given text — or not at all.

Statistically, 3,500 characters is enough to cover most everyday text — studies have shown they account for 99.5% of character usage. But to avoid the awkward situation where a character outside the “common 3,500” can’t be rendered properly, the industry often sets 7,000 characters as the target size for a typeface. Some larger projects cover 27,000, or even 87,000 characters.

items.title: Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
text: Breast milk from mothers with postpartum depression may negatively impact infants’ brain development, a Chinese study has found.

The study, published Oct. 27 in the top academic journal Cell Metabolism, was led by a team at Nanjing University, in the eastern Jiangsu province. Through a mouse model, it shows, for the first time, how depression-related changes in levels of microRNA, a type of gene-regulating molecule, contained in structures called extracellular vesicles in breast milk can affect offspring brains.

Between 10% and 20% of mothers worldwide experience postpartum depression. Children of affected mothers are more likely to face challenges in cognition, language, behavior, and school performance, and are at a higher risk of developing depression themselves.

Past research has implicated genetics and the way mothers with postpartum depression bond with, and care for, their infants as contributing to this phenomenon, but the broad and long-lasting effects of postpartum depression on child development remain unclear, according to the researchers.

Because breast milk is increasingly viewed as a “signaling system orchestrating infant development,” the researchers wrote, they looked at the relationship between milk-based microRNAs and extracellular vesicles, key parts of this signaling. Because babies’ blood-brain barrier is more permeable than adults’, these vesicles can enter the brain during nursing, making its development more sensitive to diet.

The researchers compared the breast milk of 40 human mothers clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression, and 51 without, finding that those with depression had elevated levels of three types of microRNA implicated in psychiatric illness. The same was true of the breast milk of depressed mice.

To test nursing’s role in brain development, swapping mouse pups between healthy and depressed mouse mothers. Pups born to healthy mice but nursed by their depressed counterparts showed worse cognitive and emotional behavior than pups born to depressed mothers but nursed by healthy ones.

They also found that neurons in pups nursed by depressed mothers had shorter dendrites and fewer branches in the hippocampal dentate gyrus, a part of the brain believed to play a role in memory development and depression. The problems arose mainly as the neurons matured, were detectable by day 21 after birth, and persisted into adulthood, suggesting that early nursing-environment effects can last into later development.

Giving milk from depressed mothers to healthy pups was also enough to cause cognitive impairment after weaning, while milk where the vesicles had been removed had no such effect, the researchers found.

When the team inhibited Rab27a, a protein and key factor in vesicle secretion, in the mammary glands of depressed mothers, vesicle secretion fell by 58%, and the cognitive and neurodevelopmental deficits in their pups improved significantly.

items.title: 90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
text: Chinese prosecutors have exposed an invoice-trading network that illegally traded special value-added tax (VAT) invoices totaling more than 7.4 billion yuan ($1.1 billion) over three years.

Under the guise of a Shanghai-based advertising business, the group profited by issuing and charging service fees for fake invoices from shell companies it registered to customers seeking to illegally claim tax deductions — which can be claimed for special tax invoices, but not ordinary tax invoices in China — domestic media reported Tuesday.

The case has exposed major weaknesses in business-registration oversight, tax monitoring, and financial regulators’ ability to detect suspicious fund flows between affiliated company accounts, according to experts.

From June 2025 to June 2026, more than 90 criminal suspects on the case were processed by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Procuratorate, some of whom were ordered to return their illegal gains. Processing of the case is ongoing.

The group’s ringleaders, surnamed Cui and Shen, first had employees register over 70 shell companies in their own names. Invoices were then handled via three steps: a sales team first connected with customers, who transferred money to the group in order to receive invoices; then a team obtained invoices from both the operation’s registered shell companies or legitimate businesses with unused invoicing quotas; before another team returned funds to customers following invoice-fee deductions. Customers were charged a service fee of between 7% and 13% of the invoice value.

Chinese tax law requires contracts, fund transfers, invoices, and movement of goods to align. Falsely issuing invoices can result in fines of up to 500,000 yuan, while tax dodgers may be fined up to five times the underpaid tax. Both carry risks of criminal prosecution.
To circumvent the law, customers transferred the full invoice amount to the group, which then transferred the remaining funds back to the customer through a separate, third account.
The group illegally traded over 7.4 billion yuan in VAT invoices, involving more than 420 million yuan in VAT. It also conducted illegal foreign-exchange transactions totaling 420 million yuan.

“The scale of the crimes, the degree of organization, and the length of time over which they were committed were all relatively unusual,” Li Huaisheng, a professor at the School of Criminal Justice at China University of Political Science and Law, told state media outlet CCTV.

Similar cases involving companies that obtained invoices through intermediaries have made national headlines in recent years. Last year, a group allegedly used 15 shell companies to falsely issue almost 3,500 special VAT invoices totaling 300 million yuan, domestic media reported. The defendant, surnamed Li, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison and fined 500,000 yuan.

According to the State Taxation Administration, such companies often disguise themselves as consulting, advertising, or other business services in industries with low fixed-asset requirements, long industrial chains, and large transaction values, such as recycling, road freight transport, and information technology consulting.

items.title: China unveils upgraded ‘Mazu’ ocean forecasting model to boost precision in key waters
text: China unveiled version 2.0 of its independently developed "Mazu" numerical ocean forecasting model, which provides forecasts at varying resolutions across key waters worldwide to meet major national needs, including deep-sea and polar exploration and maritime passage security, CCTV News reported on Sunday.

Developed by the National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center under the Ministry of Natural Resources, the upgraded model marks a major advance in China's independent ocean forecasting capabilities, enabling more precise forecasts in strategically important maritime areas.

Ocean numerical models are core technologies underpinning marine forecasting. Since 2018, China has successively introduced the first-generation "Mazu Ocean Current" and "Mazu Ocean Wave" models. They were the country's first global operational ocean forecasting models to support GPU acceleration. Their source code was made publicly available worldwide in 2024, and the models have since been deployed in coastal provinces and cities across China.

The global forecasting system of the 2.0 version has a resolution of 5 kilometers, doubling that of its predecessor. In key waters, including China's offshore areas and the Western Pacific, the resolution has been further increased to 1 kilometer, allowing the model to more accurately capture seabed topography and hydrological characteristics in critical maritime areas.

The upgraded model retains the advantages of GPU-based high-performance computing, lightweight operation and low energy consumption. It has also successfully completed operational tests aboard China's icebreaker and research vessel Xuelong 2.

The model's overall performance has reached an internationally advanced level, according to the center. In addition to supporting various maritime production and operational activities in China, it will also facilitate international cooperation and technology transfer to Pacific island countries.

Separately, China has also been advancing the application of its independently developed "Mazu" early warning system as part of global efforts to strengthen disaster preparedness amid intensifying climate change and increasingly frequent extreme weather events.
In 2022, the UN launched the Early Warnings for All initiative, which aims to ensure that everyone on Earth is protected by early warning systems by the end of 2027.

At the opening ceremony of the 2025 World Artificial Intelligence Conference in July 2025, the China Meteorological Administration (CMA) unveiled its "Mazu" initiative, integrating traditional Chinese culture with modern technologies to establish a global early warning service network covering multiple types of disasters. The initiative shares China's experience and technological achievements in early warning services and is the world's first national-level action plan in response to the UN initiative, according to CMA.

Since its launch, the system has been put into operation in seven foreign countries - Pakistan, Ethiopia, the Solomon Islands, Jordan, Sri Lanka, Mongolia and Djibouti - while more than 40 other countries have been able to access it for trial use through cloud-based services.

items.title: China's Wang urges Middle East dialogue in meetings with Iranian, Saudi officials
The Limits of China’s Self-Sufficiency
text: JOEL WUTHNOW is a Senior Research Fellow at the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and a co-author of China’s Quest for Military Supremacy. The views expressed here are his own.
Why the Country’s Food Insecurity Could Prevent a War Over Taiwan

When assessing the probability of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait, analysts tend to focus on a few obvious risks that China would face—namely, military defeat, economic slowdown, and restricted oil and technology imports. All of these are important, but an equally significant vulnerability is often left off the list: China’s reliance on soybean imports.

Beijing recognizes this liability. At the 20th Party Congress, in 2022, Chinese leader Xi Jinping identified “ensuring the security of food, energy resources, and critical industrial supply chains” as issues essential to national security and social stability. Food security, conspicuously listed first, is an especially sensitive issue for China’s 1.4 billion inhabitants: roughly 15 percent of the country’s population today was alive during the 1959–61 famine, which resulted in an estimated 30 million deaths.

As with technology and oil, Beijing has tried to limit its dependence on soybeans by building up stockpiles and diversifying its sources. But because soybeans are a fragile foodstuff, there is only so much China can do. Beijing can support a war effort, therefore, for only as long as the Chinese public could put the People’s Liberation Army’s success above its nutritional needs. And the key for deterring Chinese leaders from starting a conflict is to convince them that a domestic crisis would arrive sooner than any battlefield victory.

Disruption to critical imports is one of the most powerful deterrents to China’s use of force, and it’s a threat that the Chinese government has spent decades working to counter. The specter of a foreign blockade in the Strait of Malacca, through which most of Chinese oil imports pass, has worried Chinese leaders since at least 2003, when Chinese leader Hu Jintao warned about the risk of major powers’ interference creating a “Malacca dilemma” for China’s energy security. Beijing, however, has stockpiled massive reserves of oil, which it could complement in a crisis by increasing imports of Russian oil and, as Moscow has done, building up a sanctions-evading shadow fleet to transport oil from the Middle East.

Access to foreign technology is a newer but just as important concern, and China is similarly stockpiling critical components, such as chips. It is also having success in developing local alternatives. Beijing has already pulled ahead in some sectors, such as solar and battery manufacturing, or it is working to close the gap in others, as in semiconductors.

items.title: China rolls out support measures to aid struggling stocks
China to Boost Use of Stock Support Tools to Stabilize Market
China is attacking the foundations of the US economic boom
text: Matthew Field is a Senior Technology Reporter covering the UK tech sector. He has covered social media giants, technology policy and British start-ups for The Telegraph since 2017. He also writes about the space industry. He can be reached at matthew.field@telegraph.co.uk or via X @matthfield
Tim Creswick, a London-based technology entrepreneur, spent much of last week tinkering with a collection of half a dozen AI bots he uses to run his personal life.
Among the AI in his toolkit is Qwen, a cheap Chinese system from Alibaba, which he runs on his own Nvidia processors.
Relying on Qwen for simple tasks or routine coding has “more than halved” the amount he is spending on more powerful models, such as those from Anthropic and OpenAI.
Using the most powerful “frontier” bots from Anthropic or OpenAI to sort your emails or write some notes is a bit “like using a Ferrari to pick up the shopping”, Creswick says.
Like many founders who live and breathe AI, Creswick has found Chinese bots to be a useful tool to keep costs down. Their popularity is growing fast.
But, as the tech world awaits Claude developer Anthropic’s $2tn (£1.5tn) stock market float, the rapid advances of Chinese rivals are casting a shadow over Silicon Valley.
Beijing-based Moonshot, the company behind the Kimi bot, is said to be preparing a float that would value it at up to $50bn early next year.
DeepSeek, a Chinese lab with its own eponymous chatbot, is plotting its own float and was lately valued at almost $75bn.
Both DeepSeek and Moonshot were founded just three years ago. OpenAI took close to a decade to reach a similar valuation.

Their growth comes amid growing pressure over US tech valuations. The Nasdaq dropped close to 3pc on Friday while Google’s parent company recorded a record $500bn sell-off a day earlier, driven by growing unease that the spending plans of the AI industry will fail to translate into sustainable revenues.

Chinese AI companies pose a key threat. While they remain a step behind Anthropic and its rival OpenAI in terms of performance, they have been seeking to usurp Silicon Valley’s market dominance by making AI cheaper than ever.

And although Anthropic’s most powerful technology is widely regarded as still being a cut above the best that China can offer, the gap has been closing. The US’s lead over China was once a year, then six months and now perhaps just weeks.
Both Anthropic and ChatGPT developer OpenAI have been forced to trim their prices in response to China’s brutal price war.
More fundamentally, China has pioneered work on so-called “open-weight” AI tools, which can be freely downloaded and tweaked by users.
Those with some technical knowledge can run them on their own hardware, rather than via the cloud, bringing down costs further.

Last week, DeepSeek revealed a new open-source AI system known as DeepInfer. It effectively offers free access to technology the company uses in its internal AI systems, aimed at helping businesses and expert users to bring down their costs.
Silicon Valley’s leading AI tools, on the other hand, are normally run on systems with guardrails and settings tightly controlled by the labs themselves.

items.title: UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
text: Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed
The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.

An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
Liam Byrne, Labour MP and chair of the committee said the UK’s policy on China meant it was also endangering its business with the EU with the risk of being “cut off” from big manufacuring contracts.
The government could neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control the “increasing exposure to unquantified, managed risk” in relations with China, it found.
The report said: “In 2024, the new government promised a strategic, long-term, consistent UK approach to China. It has not delivered on this.
“Britain must shape its own relationship with China or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.”
The UK’s relationship with China has been marked by a lack of engagement in the last 10 years, with Keir Starmer making the first official visit in January since Theresa May in 2018.

That trip was billed as an effort to end the “diplomatic ice age”, but since 2018 China has benefited from an export boom that is now fuelling fears about deindustrialisation, adding to deep-seated existing concerns about cyber espionage and national security.

The MPs acknowledged the advantages of trading with Beijing in their report, noting that British businesses have profitable operations in China and “are ambitious to grow” and learn from the country’s “world-leading” innovations.
At the same time, consumers benefit from low-cost imports when household incomes are squeezed, with electric vehicles being a case in point.
However, Byrne sharply criticised the government’s piecemeal approach.
“Britain’s businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.
“Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the 11th hour.”
The committee cited the decision in March to block the Chinese firm Ming Yang from building a £1.5bn wind energy plant in Scotland after years of negotiation because of unspecified security risks.
Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, has called on Andy Burnham to reconsider Starmer’s decision.
That decision, along with the emergency takeover of British Steel from its Chinese owners, “has been characterised by reactivity, inconsistency and opacity”, the report said.

Work on a new strategy, the committee said, should be combined with official preparations for new trade remedies to counter unfair competition, including potential tariffs on EVs, something Downing Street has not ruled out.

The report calls for “clear new rules of the game” and recommends the designation of a “red zone” for industries that would be off-limits for Chinese investment and a “green zone”, where trade should be encouraged.

items.title: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
text: The government has failed to deliver on its promise to pursue a consistent approach towards China and is instead making up policy "as it goes along", MPs on the business committee have said.
The committee said in its report that decision-making had been characterised by "inconsistency" and was heightening national security risks.
It called on ministers to block the transfer of sensitive data to China, give businesses clear rules for doing trade with the super power and ban imports made using forced labour.
The business department said it disagreed with the report's conclusion adding: "Our approach to China is consistent - we will co-operate where we can and challenge where we must."
"We have placed our relationship on a more stable, balanced, long-term footing, and based it on a clear-eyed assessment of both the opportunities and the risks.

"Our trade strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on our national security, and our increased discussions with China allows us to directly raise concerns where they arise."

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had sought to pursue a closer relationship with China, arguing that the UK could not afford to ignore economic opportunities, while insisting that should not mean compromising on national security.
However, efforts to build ties were criticised by some MPs concerned about China's alleged spying activities in the UK.
An audit of the two countries' relationship was carried out last year but the government has not published the document in full, saying it contained classified information.
Sir Keir's successor Andy Burnham has yet to set out his position on relations with China.

In its report, the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee said successive governments had "failed to reassure" the public they had taken "adequate measures to defend UK national security and economic resilience".
The MPs said the unpredictability of government approaches and a lack of clear guidance had hindered businesses ability to trade with China.
It proposed setting up "red" and "green" zones to clearly defining where trade and investment would be encouraged and the areas which were "off limits".

The committee said that the government should insist on fair trade with China and advised preparing tariffs that could be imposed if the country continued to subsidise its industry or failed to offer "fully reciprocal" market access.
On protecting sensitive technology and data, the report said there should be a ban on connected technology devices being used in critical national infrastructure.

The committee said "low-cost" Chinese connected technology had become wide-spread in the UK and that in this area the government had "prioritised diplomatic politeness over the UK's national security".
Universities should also get "faster advice" on conducting research with Chinese bodies, it said.
Committee chair and Labour MP Liam Byrne said: "Britain's businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.

items.title: China Factory Activity Expands But Ends Streak of Faster Growth
Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain, some carrying eggs and watermelons
text: Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks Monday, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
For hundreds of years, Mount Tai -- the tallest peak in China's eastern Shandong province -- was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors, and it features prominently in Chinese mythology.

But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.
The UNESCO World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.

Over a 2.4-mile course with more than 1,970 feet of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.
A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology -- a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree -- completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.
Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.
The fastest humanoid robot -- belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue -- completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.
Organizers called Mount Tai's rocky terrain a "natural extreme testing ground" that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.
The race, organized by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.
